title: Android Architecture Layers
body: Android is the world's most popular mobile OS. It is open-source (AOSP) and highly customizable, used by manufacturers like Samsung, Google, and Xiaomi. Layered architecture: Linux Kernel at the bottom, followed by Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL), Android Runtime (ART/Dalvik), Native C++ libraries, and the Java/Kotlin Application Framework. Uses a sandboxed environment for apps. Each app runs in its own process with a unique user ID. Uses Intents for inter-process communication.

title: CPU Architecture
body: The CPU performs most of the processing inside the computer. It executes instructions of a computer program by performing basic arithmetic, logic, controlling, and input/output operations. Modern CPUs use the Von Neumann or Harvard architectures. Key components include the ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit), CU (Control Unit), Registers, and Cache hierarchy (L1, L2, L3). CPUs operate on the fetch-decode-execute cycle. The Control Unit fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it into commands, and the ALU executes them.

title: GPU Architecture
body: GPUs are highly parallel processors originally designed for rendering graphics, now widely used for AI, machine learning, and scientific simulations. GPUs consist of thousands of smaller, simpler cores compared to CPUs. Architectures like Nvidia's Hopper or AMD's RDNA feature Streaming Multiprocessors, Tensor Cores, and RT Cores. GPUs excel at SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) operations, applying the same instruction to multiple data points simultaneously, ideal for pixel rendering and matrix math.

title: Graphics Card — Guide
body: A graphics card (also called a discrete GPU or video card) is an expansion card that installs into a PCIe slot on the motherboard. It has its own dedicated GPU chip, VRAM, power delivery, and cooling — offloading all rendering tasks from the CPU and integrated graphics. Modern graphics cards include hardware ray tracing units, dedicated AI tensor cores (NVIDIA) or matrix accelerators (AMD), and support technologies like DLSS 3 and FSR 3 for AI-powered upscaling. The NVIDIA RTX 4090 has 16,384 CUDA cores and 76 billion transistors. It's so powerful that it can render 60fps at 8K resolution in some games — a resolution most monitors don't even support yet. title: HDD — Hard Disk Drive
body: A Hard Disk Drive (HDD) stores data on spinning magnetic platters. A read/write head moves across the platters to access data. HDDs are much slower than SSDs but offer enormous storage at very low cost — making them ideal for backups, NAS systems, and bulk media storage. IBM introduced the first HDD in 1956 — it weighed over 900 kg, held 5 MB of data, and cost $10,000 per month to lease. Today, you can buy 20 TB for under ₹25,000. title: Microphone — Audio Input Guide
body: A microphone is an input device that converts sound (air pressure waves) into electrical signals. Used for voice calls, podcasting, streaming, recording music, voice assistants, and gaming communication. The two main transducer types are condenser (sensitive, studio-quality) and dynamic (rugged, handles loud volumes). title: Motherboard Chipset
body: The motherboard holds and allows communication between many of the crucial electronic components of a system, such as the CPU and memory, and provides connectors for other peripherals. Includes the CPU socket, RAM slots, PCIe slots, chipset (Northbridge/Southbridge historically, now highly integrated PCH), VRMs (Voltage Regulator Modules), and I/O ports. Traces on the PCB act as buses, routing data and power. The chipset manages data flow between the CPU, memory, and peripherals using protocols like PCIe, SATA, and USB.

title: NPU — Neural Processing Unit
body: A Neural Processing Unit (NPU), also known as an AI Accelerator or Tensor Processing Unit (TPU), is a specialized microprocessor designed specifically to accelerate the math required for machine learning algorithms, particularly artificial neural networks. While CPUs are optimized for low-latency serial processing, and GPUs for highly parallel graphical pixel rendering, NPUs are optimized for dense matrix multiplication and convolution operations. They execute low-precision math (like INT8, FP16, BF16) at staggering speeds, dramatically reducing the time and power required to train or infer with large AI models. Modern NPUs use systolic arrays, a hardware architecture where data flows through a grid of arithmetic logic units (ALUs) in a pipelined fashion, minimizing the need to fetch data from memory repeatedly. title: Optical Laser Technology
body: While now a legacy component for mainstream users, optical drives use precise laser technology to access data encoded as microscopic pits and lands on a polycarbonate disc. Consists of a spindle motor, a tracking mechanism, and an optical pickup head containing a semiconductor laser diode and photodiode sensor. A laser beam is focused onto the spinning disc. Changes in reflection from pits (indentations) and lands (flat areas) are detected by the photodiode and translated into binary data.

title: OS Kernel Architecture
body: The Operating System (OS) is the most critical software in a computer. It bridges the gap between hardware and user applications, handling memory management, process scheduling, file systems, and hardware abstraction. Modern OS architecture centers around the Kernel (Monolithic, Microkernel, or Hybrid). It includes the hardware abstraction layer (HAL), system call interface, and user space applications. The OS kernel operates in privileged mode (Ring 0), directly controlling CPU scheduling, memory allocation (paging/segmentation), and hardware interrupts via device drivers.

title: PSU — Power Supply Unit
body: The Power Supply Unit (PSU) converts AC power from your wall outlet into the DC voltages (3.3V, 5V, 12V) that your computer components require. title: Quantum Computing
body: Classical computers encode information in Bits, which strictly hold a value of 0 or 1. A Quantum Computer encodes information in Qubits (Quantum Bits), which operate based on the principles of quantum mechanics. Due to phenomena like superposition and entanglement, qubits can represent 0, 1, or any quantum superposition of these states simultaneously. This allows quantum computers to perform massive multi-dimensional computations at once, scaling exponentially. While a classical 100-bit state represents exactly one of $2^{100}$ possible states, a 100-qubit state represents a probability distribution across all $2^{100}$ states simultaneously. In 1994, Peter Shor formulated an algorithm that can theoretically factor large prime numbers exponentially faster than any known classical algorithm. If a large enough stable quantum computer is built, it will break modern RSA encryption overnight. Superposition A quantum system remains in a linear combination of multiple states until measured. A

title: RAM Architecture
body: RAM provides high-speed, volatile data storage for the CPU. It is essential for multitasking and quick data retrieval during program execution. RAM consists of memory cells built from a capacitor and a transistor. Cells are organized into arrays (banks), accessed via rows and columns by memory controllers. The CPU sends a memory address to the memory controller, which activates the corresponding row and column. The data is read by sense amplifiers and sent to the CPU.

title: Raspberry Pi & SBCs

Unlike traditional motherboards, SBCs do not rely on expansion slots for peripheral functions. The Raspberry Pi, launched in 2012, is the most famous SBC. These pins allow the computer to directly read sensors (temperature, light) and control physical components (motors, LEDs) using code like Python. title: Central Processing Unit Deep Data
body: The CPU performs most of the processing inside the computer. It executes instructions of a computer program by performing basic arithmetic, logic, controlling, and input/output operations. Modern CPUs use the Von Neumann or Harvard architectures. Key components include the ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit), CU (Control Unit), Registers, and Cache hierarchy (L1, L2, L3). The first commercial microprocessor was the Intel 4004, released in 1971. Over decades, CPUs evolved from single-core processors to multi-core giants, adhering to Moore's Law for many years. CPUs operate on the fetch-decode-execute cycle. The Control Unit fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it into commands, and the ALU executes them. Interrupt-driven architecture. The executive layer handles memory management, process management, and I/O. The user-mode environment facilitates application execution via APIs.
